Hilbert and Moore Curves

SequencesAlgorithmsInvariants
Game: Watch a single line snake through every small square of a grid.
How to play: Move the slider to make the curve more detailed, and switch between Hilbert and Moore.
Look for the math

A curve that never crosses itself can still pass arbitrarily close to every point of a square. The trick is to take a limit of finite curves.

Four copies of the previous curve

Start with a staple-shaped path through four cells. To get the next order, shrink the path, place four copies in the quadrants — the lower two as they are, the upper two turned a quarter turn in opposite directions — and join them with short segments. Order n visits every cell of a 2ⁿ × 2ⁿ grid exactly once. The Hilbert curve starts at a corner; the Moore curve joins the ends into a closed loop.

What the check found

The logic test checks orders 1 through 6: each curve visits every cell once, all points stay in the square, and consecutive points are always neighbours. The page stresses that no finite curve fills the square — only the limiting curve does, which must self-intersect. The logic test describes the finite stages only, which is what the applet draws.

Set the order to 6 and switch to Moore. Can you spot where the loop closes?
